summary: This incident report reviews seasonal patterns of weather-related utility outages in fall and winter 2023 and how utilities, governments, and businesses respond. It covers forecasting, smart grid technology, communication, microgrids, inter-agency cooperation, business continuity planning, and infrastructure reinforcement. It concludes that climate change makes outages inevitable, so proactive adaptation is needed.
one_line: Report on fall and winter 2023 weather-related utility outages and strategies for preparation, response, technology, communication, and infrastructure resilience.
key_facts: On October 12, 2023, a powerful storm swept through the Midwest, leaving over 200,000 homes without power.
On November 19, 2023, the Northeast had unseasonably early snowfall that brought down power lines and hindered road transportation.
On December 5, a severe ice storm in the New England area caused outages affecting over 300,000 homes and businesses.
James Walker, a line crew supervisor for the Midwestern Power & Light Company, said his crews staged equipment in known trouble spots before the first snowflake hit the ground.
Angela Pearson, an energy analyst for Northeastern Grid Operations, said artificial intelligence helps predict outage locations from weather patterns and historical data.
On October 28, a flash flood disrupted countless connections in the Southwest; text message alerts and an updated emergency website kept residents informed.
Microgrids can operate independently from the primary power grid and supply electricity to a specific area, increasing resilience against general grid failures.
On September 21, an unprecedented storm required a unified response from utility companies, first responders, and emergency management teams, according to Jane Mckenzie.
Businesses are adopting resilience strategies including backup generators, off-site data storage, and flexible work arrangements.
Marcus Li, owner of a local manufacturing firm, said a power backup system kept his production line active during outages.
Long-term infrastructure measures include burying power lines, upgrading to more robust materials, and proactive tree-trimming programs.
Structural engineer Lauren Blackwell said it is better to invest now in weather-resistant infrastructure than to repeatedly suffer the consequences of outdated systems.
The report attributes increasing severity and unpredictability of weather patterns to climate change.
